<LinkCard title="Determinism" href="/explanation/determinism" description="What the byte-identical guarantee rests on." />


## Concepts

Architecture, determinism, performance, and size doctrine.

### Architecture
Source: /explanation/architecture

import { Aside, Code, FileTree, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Takumi Motion is a bridge between two worlds: high-level React (or raw HTML) authoring, and a Rust rasterizer that renders CSS-style layouts natively. The bridge is deliberately narrow — a JSON timeline, a static markup tree per frame, and integer milliseconds.

## The pipeline

<Code lang="text" code={`AUTHOR    React components or templates produce a node tree + TimelineJSON
PLAN      Scene windows, transitions, and frame grids resolve up front
CAPTURE   Each frame renders to static markup (pure function of frame index)
COMPILE   The timeline bakes onto a shared fps grid (CSS keyframes)
RASTER    The Rust engine (takumi) renders markup + styles to pixels
ENCODE    GIF / WebP / APNG encoders emit files; post-processing runs`} />

Four properties hold everywhere:

- **Determinism** — `Math.random` is frame-seeded, engine time is integer ms, and no network or clock reads happen during render. Same input, same bytes.
- **Ahead-of-time timelines** — nothing animates "live". The engine samples authored tracks at frame indices and merges byte-identical frames into chunks.
- **Rust rasterization** — the takumi engine (via `@takumi-rs/core`, a prebuilt native module) lays out and paints each frame; no headless browser exists in the pipeline.
- **The report is the API** — every render returns its files, budgets, lint findings, seam verdict, and timings as data.

## Capture lifecycle in detail

<Code lang="text" code={`PROBE    <Banner> registers meta + scene inputs (children do not render yet)
PLAN     planBanner() computes frame-exact scene windows
PREWARM  each scene's opening frame renders once (FitText/Morph discovery;
      outputs are discarded — components may see one extra render per scene)
FRAMES   the real per-frame loop produces the markup that gets encoded
CHUNK    byte-identical adjacent frames merge
LINT     style trees + markup + registry findings assemble report.lint`} />

The prewarm pass is why `<FitText>` and `<Morph>` can measure through the real renderer and still render synchronously in the frame loop. Prewarm outputs never reach the encoder.

## Source surface map

<FileTree>
- src/content/docs (site pages)
- takumi-motion (the package)
  - index.ts — root export: engine + renderers + audit + kit
  - react/ — primitives, hooks, capture runtime, parallel workers
  - templates/ — the four banner recipes
  - cli.ts — the terminal surface
</FileTree>

The package's public surface splits by intent:

| Concern | Where it lives |
| --- | --- |
| Authoring in React | `takumi-motion/react` |
| Authoring without React | `createTimeline` + `h` (root) or `takumi-motion/recipes` |
| Rendering | `renderBanner`, `renderReactBanner`, `renderHtmlAnimation`, `renderStill`, sprite/sequence exporters |
| Verification | `renderWithAudit`, `checkBanner`, `auditExtents`, lint channel, `explainCapture` |
| Terminal | the `takumi-motion` binary |

## Why not a browser?

A headless browser brings nondeterminism (font hinting, timers, layout races), heavy startup cost, and a byte-output floor. The Rust engine renders the same CSS subset natively and fast — the v1.0 benchmarks record an 80-frame banner end-to-end in ~37 ms, serial. The trade is a bounded style property set (`SUPPORTED_STYLE_PROPS`), which the type system and the `TM_UNKNOWN_STYLE_PROP` lint make explicit.

<Aside type="note">
  This docs site is itself a separate codebase (Astro Starlight). The repository you clone contains the engine; the site ships in its own archive with its own build.
</Aside>

## Next steps

<LinkCard title="Determinism" href="/explanation/determinism" description="The frame model that makes byte-exact output possible." />

<LinkCard title="Performance & Size" href="/explanation/performance-and-size" description="What the Velocity pass changed and why it matters." />

### Determinism
Source: /explanation/determinism

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

"Deterministic" is the product. This page explains the mechanisms that make every render byte-reproducible — and the rules your code must follow to keep them intact.

## The frame model

Every frame is a pure function of `(frame, props)`:

- Frames are integers. Time enters the engine only as whole milliseconds (`toEngineMs` clamps and floors at every boundary — fractional `timeMs` is rejected by the Rust side).
- Hooks and components read the frame, never the clock: `useFrame()`, `useCurrentFrame()`, `useAbsoluteFrame()`. There is no `Date.now()` in the runtime and none is allowed in your components.
- Replays are exact: frame 137 of a render is identical to frame 137 of any other render of the same input, whether it happens locally, in CI, or inside a worker window.

## Seeded randomness

`Math.random()` is shimmed during capture to `mulberry32(seed ⊕ imul(frame))` — each frame's PRNG stream starts fresh from its own seed. Consequences:

- Random motion (particles, wiggle, confetti) replays byte-identically at any frame index, in any order, across any number of workers.
- The v1.0 shim is per-frame: a stream does not continue across frames. Code that consumed growing randomness across frames must seed explicitly (`useRandom(seed, salt)`).
- Authoring code should use `useRandom`/`randomFor` directly — calling `Math.random` works only while the shim covers it and hides the seed from the system.

## Integer engine time and the fps grid

The compile step bakes every track onto a shared fps grid plus structural boundaries, so the engine sees whole-millisecond times only. Springs are the exception worth knowing: they are solved analytically per sample (no grid), with settle thresholds from Motion's physics (`restSpeed`, `restDelta`). `springSettleFrames(fps, options)` tells you when a spring stops moving visually — if that exceeds the scene window, the `TM_TRANSITION_UNSETTLED` lint fires.

## The determinism probe

`renderWithAudit` renders twice and byte-compares the first poster:

<Code lang="json" code={`{
    "determinism": {
  "deterministic": true,
  "checkedBytes": 18432,
  "detail": "poster @ 1500ms byte-identical across renders"
    }
}`} />

`deterministic: false` is a hard alarm — it means an input varied between renders. The usual culprits, in order of likelihood:

1. A network fetch or `Date.now()` inside a render function.
2. Remote (Google) fonts — their bytes can change upstream; vendor TTF/OTF locally (the `TM_FONT_NETWORK` lint warns).
3. Unseeded `Math.random` outside the shimmed capture stages.

## Parallel capture keeps the promise

Workers render frame windows concurrently, yet output stays byte-identical to serial capture at any worker count. The mechanisms:

- Plan agreement — every worker asserts it derived the same scene plan before rendering.
- Frame-seeded randomness (above) — window boundaries cannot shift PRNG streams.
- Single re-merge — windows concatenate and re-chunk once on the main thread.

The repository's golden tests assert this invariant, and `renderWithAudit`'s probe verifies it per render.

<Aside type="caution">
  Determinism is why some conveniences are absent: no live clocks, no network fetches at render, no unseeded randomness, no WOFF fonts (their bytes would have to be trusted upstream). Each restriction buys a byte-exact guarantee.
</Aside>

### Performance & Size
Source: /explanation/performance-and-size

import { Aside, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The v1.0 release ("Velocity") is a performance pass over the frozen v0.9.1 pipeline, differential-tested byte-identical — every optimization changed speed, never output. This page records what changed, the measured wins, and the size doctrine that guides the encoders.

## What got faster

The pipeline is React/HTML → `renderToStaticMarkup` per frame → chunk merge → `fromHtml` (napi) → `renderAnimation` (Rust, rayon) → encode → post-process. The Velocity pass removed four classes of waste:

| Change | Mechanism | Hot path |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solver memoization | Spring generators and settle durations memoize on transition params | `springFor` — every Animated/spring per frame |
| Binary-search tween sampling | Per-segment easings precomputed once; O(log n) segment lookup | compile bake, evaluators |
| Identity-memoized tracks | `resolveTrack` memoizes on object identity (WeakMap); target-indexed transform maps | `evaluateAt` |
| Color parse memo | `parseToRgba` results memoize (bounded) | per-frame color mixing |
| Structural compile dedupe | fps grid built once and shared; structural step dedupe replaces per-point `JSON.stringify` | `compileTimeline` |
| Binary-search chunk index | One shared O(log n) frame→chunk helper | posters, sequences, sprite sheets, filmstrips, storyboards |
| Zero-copy GIF passes | `subarray` views + native `memcmp` (`Buffer#equals`) for holds ≥ 64 bytes | GIF hold collapse |
| PNG min-SAD filter | Standard minimum-sum-of-absolute-differences per-row filter heuristic + deflate level 9 | sprite/sequence encoders |

## Measured (Node 24, linux x64, median of 9 runs)

| Bench | Baseline | v1.0 | Speedup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Chunk index: 200k lookups over 400 chunks | 37.4 ms | 5.3 ms | **7.07×** |
| Spring: 3000 samples, 20 configs | 4.4 ms | 1.1 ms | **3.87×** |
| evaluateAt: 400 sweeps × 5 tracks | 2.8 ms | 0.9 ms | **3.14×** |
| Color mix: 50k mixes | 25.4 ms | 9.6 ms | **2.65×** |
| Capture: 80-frame banner (probe→chunk) | 6.6 ms | 3.6 ms | **1.84×** |
| End-to-end: 80f banner, serial | 53.5 ms | 37.3 ms | **1.43×** |
| PNG atlas bytes (850×400 gradient) | 767 KiB | 2.0 KiB | **−100%** |
| **Geometric mean (13 timed benches)** | | | **1.71×** |

Two honest losses: PNG encode CPU rose 33% on the atlas bench (the min-SAD heuristic costs time to save bytes), and `workers: 4` on a 2-core host measured 0.88× — the reason the auto gate exists.

## The size doctrine

Encoded size is per-frame delta × frames. The engine's design keeps both terms low:

- **Settled descriptors emit nothing.** Once an enter/exit transition or spring settles, wrappers stop emitting style overrides, so identical frames chunk-merge into zero-delta holds. The GIF pass rewrites holds as longer frame delays; the report's `collapse` block quantifies it.
- **Finite churn only.** Confetti bursts settle at `burstFrames`; unbounded fields trip `TM_PARTICLE_CHURN`. A GIF that never stops moving never compresses.
- **Integer, quantized values.** Emitted values round to 6 decimals; color outputs are integer-channel `rgb()` — palette quantizers round anyway, and stable values keep the chunk-merger effective.
- **Cheap channels preferred.** Opacity and clip changes are cheap; layout, text, and structure churn re-encode whole regions. The X-ray (`--explain`) attributes each frame to its channel so you can see which term you are paying for.
- **Format choice is a size lever.** WebP for gradients and glow, dpr 2 when host platforms re-compress anyway, `readme-lean` when bytes dominate. The [size guide](/guides/reduce-file-size) turns each lever into steps.

<Aside type="note">
  The benchmarks live in the repository (`docs/BENCHMARKS.md`) with the frozen baseline in `bench/baseline/` — a verbatim copy of the v0.9.1 tree — so every number above is reproducible from the source.
</Aside>

## Home (/)

import { Aside, Card, CardGrid, LinkButton, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Takumi Motion compiles animation timelines ahead of time, captures frames deterministically, and delegates rasterization to a Rust backend. No headless browser, no layout thrashing, no nondeterministic replays — the same input produces the same bytes, every time.

## Why Takumi Motion

- **Deterministic by construction** — `Math.random` is frame-seeded, engine time is integer milliseconds, and every frame is a pure function of `(frame, props)`. Outputs are byte-identical across runs, worker counts, and machines.
- **Rust-fast rendering** — the takumi engine rasterizes CSS-style layouts in native code. The v1.0 *Velocity* pass lifted the hot path by a geometric mean of **1.71×** across 13 benchmarks.
- **Author in React** — banners are ordinary React trees with `<Scene>` and `<Layer>` primitives, Motion-compatible springs and easings, and frame-driven hooks.
- **Quality tooling built in** — a coded authoring lint (`TM_*`), per-frame X-ray attribution, extent auditing, and loop-seam verification ride along with every render report.

<Aside type="tip">
  Read [Determinism](/explanation/determinism) if you have ever shipped an animated banner that rendered differently in CI than locally — Takumi Motion removes that entire class of bug.
</Aside>
